objectives.title: Strategy and business opportunity
objectives.description: Explain a strategic approach to digital marketing opportunities and challenges.

objectives.title: Audiences, platforms and media
objectives.description: Review digital media and platform options for communications goals.

objectives.title: Data and technology
objectives.description: Explain how data and technology support audience experiences and business goals.

modules.title: Start with the customer, not the tool
modules.subtitle: Digital marketing, integration and the 7Ds
objectives: Explain digital marketing as a means to an objective.
Connect the seven pillars without confusing a device, platform and channel.
Distinguish digital business from e-commerce.
summary: Choose the customer and business result before a technology.
Digital and offline touchpoints support one journey.
The 7Ds are connected planning dimensions.
E-commerce includes informational exchanges, not only checkout.

diagram.title: A connected planning system
diagram.relation: Goals guide choices; customer evidence feeds improvements across all seven pillars.

case.title: The app-first trap
case.context: Hypothetical scenario: a campus stationery shop has a queue at lunchtime and an outdated online stock list.
case.problem: The owner wants an expensive app immediately. What is the strongest first move?
options: Buy the app and decide its purpose later.
Clarify the customer problem, service objective and channel handoff.
Move the entire service to social media.
explanations: A tool-first approach can leave the actual customer problem unresolved.
Map the need, define a useful outcome and then select the least complex suitable technology.
Changing platform does not resolve inaccurate stock or the queue.

modules.title: Turn ambition into a plan
modules.subtitle: RACE, 5Ss and the strategy feedback loop
objectives: Choose RACE measures that match the lifecycle stage.
Use the 5Ss to broaden a business case.
Connect opportunity, strategy, action and measurement.
summary: RACE connects acquisition and retention.
Act means meaningful interaction; Convert concerns sales.
5Ss describe benefits rather than five lifecycle stages.
An OVP explains the distinctive online benefit.
Measurement informs objectives and strategy again.

diagram.title: Strategy is a learning loop
diagram.relation: Evidence loops back to opportunity and strategy; the phases inform one another.

case.title: Reach is not the bottleneck
case.context: Hypothetical scenario: a service business attracts visitors, but very few request a useful consultation.
case.problem: Which initial plan best addresses the observed gap?
options: Buy more impressions without changing the journey.
Review Act-stage friction and the relevance of the consultation offer.
Report visits as completed sales.
explanations: More reach may amplify the same problem.
Check the offer, interaction and handoff, then choose a measure such as qualified enquiries.
Visits and sales are different lifecycle outcomes.

modules.title: Choose a viable digital business
modules.subtitle: Digital presence, growth and strategic risk
objectives: Match online functionality to a business contribution.
Distinguish three ways digital channels can grow demand.
Use historical cases without assuming a guaranteed recipe.
summary: Not every website needs online checkout.
Five presence functions can coexist.
Growth may mean new category users, switching or deeper relationships.
Capability, cost, attention and integration constrain execution.
Boo.com and Boohoo.com are distinct businesses.

diagram.title: Match the presence to its job
diagram.relation: Functions may overlap. Choose and fund the combination that supports the business model.

case.title: A launch decision
case.context: Hypothetical scenario inspired by the historical Boo.com case: a retailer tests an immersive shop that works well in the office but loads poorly on customer devices.
case.problem: What should the launch team prioritise?
options: Expand into every market before testing.
Test with target customers and realistic access conditions; reassess unit economics.
Replace customer research with investor enthusiasm.
explanations: Expansion increases exposure to untested constraints.
Customer capability, delivery cost and conversion assumptions need validation.
Investor interest is not evidence of a usable customer experience.

modules.title: Meet audiences where they are
modules.subtitle: Transaction types, 6Is, devices and channels
objectives: Classify who supplies value and who receives it.
Apply the 6Is without treating digital as automatically superior.
Choose among six channel families using audience and task context.
summary: B2B, B2C, C2C and C2B depend on the transaction direction.
The 6Is explain useful communications differences.
Device and platform adoption vary across audiences.
Paid, owned and earned are media relationships, not six channel names.
Channel choice should reflect the intended action.

diagram.title: Two questions for every media choice
nodes: Search / social / ads / PR / partners / messaging
diagram.relation: Channel and media relationship are different dimensions. Match both to a customer task and lifecycle goal.

case.title: The sponsored review
case.context: Hypothetical scenario: a study-supplies brand pays a creator to show a product. Customers later share the video without payment.
case.problem: How should the team describe these communications?
options: Every third-party post is earned.
The paid placement and independent customer sharing have different media relationships.
The brand owns the social platform.
explanations: Payment distinguishes the initial placement.
The initial placement is paid; independent sharing can be earned.
An account or paid placement does not confer platform ownership.

modules.title: Build relationships beyond the campaign
modules.subtitle: Inbound, permission, content and always-on
objectives: Distinguish five related communications concepts.
Design a useful content and permission exchange.
Separate short-term interaction from sustained engagement.
summary: Inbound starts with people seeking a useful answer.
Permission requires an agreed exchange.
Content strategy includes production, distribution and governance.
Long-term engagement is more than a single reaction.
Always-on activity complements campaign bursts.

diagram.title: A useful relationship engine
diagram.relation: This learning adaptation links concepts; it is not a mandatory sequence for every customer.

case.title: Turn a download into a relationship
case.context: Hypothetical scenario: students download a free planning checklist. The team wants to build a useful ongoing relationship.
case.problem: Which follow-up best fits the chapter?
options: Send every downloader daily offers indefinitely.
Explain the optional updates, honour preferences and provide relevant follow-up.
Treat the download count as long-term loyalty.
explanations: Volume without agreement or relevance can undermine trust.
Permission and useful lifecycle content work together.
A download is an interaction; durable engagement needs further evidence.

modules.title: Make data useful, not just plentiful
modules.subtitle: Profiles, behaviour, analytics and attribution
objectives: Distinguish profile, behavioural and inferred data.
Turn a measurement question into a decision.
Explain the limitations of attributing conversions.
summary: Data is useful when it informs a defined decision.
Profiles combine disclosed details, preferences and possible inferences.
Behavioural events need reliable tracking and context.
Multiple devices and touchpoints complicate attribution.

diagram.title: From records to a better decision
diagram.relation: Learning feeds the next question. No diagram can remove missing-data or causal uncertainty.

case.title: The missing journey
case.context: Hypothetical scenario: an email receives the last click before a sale. A previous social visit occurred on another device.
options: Email caused the entire sale with certainty.
The recorded path is incomplete; assess contribution with explicit attribution limits.
Ignore all sales because attribution is imperfect.
explanations: Last-click observation is not full causal evidence.
Use the available evidence while acknowledging incomplete measurement.
Limitations require careful interpretation rather than abandoning measurement.

modules.title: Choose technology that serves the plan
modules.subtitle: Martech, integration and responsible implementation
objectives: Explain martech’s operational and insight roles.
Map the six layers in the chapter’s technology view.
Choose an integration plan around a real need.
summary: Tools can support delivery and insight.
The stack includes more than visible campaign software.
APIs and shared definitions help systems work together.
People, costs and data quality affect value from a tool.

diagram.title: The stack supports the experience
diagram.relation: Groups support one another; select only what the customer task and organisation can justify.

case.title: One useful automation
case.context: Hypothetical scenario: a small service team has inconsistent customer details and is considering several new automation tools.
case.problem: Which next step best follows Chapter 1?
options: Purchase all the tools before reviewing the data.
Define a useful customer task, data owner, integration needs and a small evaluated pilot.
Automate all messages regardless of preferences.
explanations: More tools may multiply the current inconsistency.
Goal-led implementation tests whether technology creates value.
Relevance and preferences remain necessary.

concepts.definition: Use digital media, data and technology, alongside other marketing activities, to achieve marketing objectives.
points: Start with the desired acquisition, service, retention or brand outcome.
A website, app or social account is a means, not proof of marketing effectiveness.
Customer relationship management supports continued use and relationships after acquisition.
concepts.example: A hypothetical campus shop improves access to product information before choosing whether it needs an app.
concepts.mistake: Buying software is not itself a marketing strategy.
concepts.recall: Which proposal best expresses digital marketing?
answer: Name a customer or business objective.
Explain the role of media, data and technology.
Include offline integration when the audience needs it.

quiz.prompt: Which proposal best expresses digital marketing?
options: Use digital touchpoints to increase relevant enquiries and improve service.
Replace every physical interaction with a screen.
Launch an app because competitors have one.
explanations: The objective leads the choice of digital activities.
Digital marketing can support offline interactions too.
This names a tool without a result.

concepts.definition: Coordinate online and offline touchpoints so customers can progress through their relationship with the organisation.
points: A person may research online and buy in a shop, or do the reverse.
Align information, handoffs and service across web, phone, email and staff.
AIDA explains a response sequence; RACE also addresses ongoing retention.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: a student checks stock on a website, asks a question by chat and collects the product at a shop.
concepts.mistake: A website sale total alone can miss the website’s contribution to offline sales.
concepts.recall: A website visit leads to an in-store purchase. What should the marketer consider?
answer: Describe the channel handoff.
Explain why the website can contribute without taking payment.
Use measures appropriate to each touchpoint.

quiz.prompt: A website visit leads to an in-store purchase. What should the marketer consider?
options: The website failed because it did not take payment.
The digital and shop experience should be assessed together.
The shop should stop serving customers offline.
explanations: Research and lead generation can support offline conversion.
The complete journey matters.
Integration preserves useful offline choices.

concepts.definition: Seven connected dimensions organise digital marketing: goals, audiences, devices, platforms, media, data and technology.
points: Goals guide the result; audiences describe the people.
Devices are access hardware; platforms mediate interactions.
Media carry communications, data supports understanding, and technology supports delivery and insight.
The pillars form a connected audit, not seven guaranteed stages of success.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: for a phone user arriving from a search platform, paid search is the media technique; the analytics and content systems are supporting technology.
concepts.mistake: A smartphone, a search engine and paid search are related but different categories.
concepts.recall: Which item is a digital device?
answer: List all seven dimensions.
Distinguish physical access, interaction platform and communications technique.
Explain how goals guide the other dimensions.

quiz.prompt: Which item is a digital device?
options: A paid search campaign.
A customer profile.
A smartphone.
explanations: This is a media technique.
This is data about a customer.
This is access hardware.

concepts.definition: E-commerce covers electronically mediated financial and informational exchanges with external parties; digital business also includes internal processes.
points: Sell-side concerns exchanges with customers; buy-side concerns procurement from suppliers.
An enquiry or service exchange can be e-commerce even without an online payment.
Transactional e-commerce is the narrower everyday sense of selling online.
Social commerce uses participation such as reviews, ratings or group buying to support shopping.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: an online supplier order is buy-side; a customer booking is sell-side; internal stock processing belongs to the wider digital business.
concepts.mistake: Do not treat e-commerce, online sales and all digital business processes as identical.
concepts.recall: Which activity is buy-side e-commerce?
answer: State the broad and narrow meanings of e-commerce.
Contrast buy-side and sell-side.
Explain why digital business is broader.

quiz.prompt: Which activity is buy-side e-commerce?
options: A company orders packaging from its supplier online.
A shopper buys the company’s product.
Two staff discuss an internal rota.
explanations: The company is purchasing resources.
This is sell-side from the company’s perspective.
Internal coordination belongs to broader digital business.

concepts.definition: Reach, Act, Convert and Engage organise activities and measures across the customer lifecycle.
points: Reach builds awareness and visits; Act encourages useful interactions and leads.
Convert concerns sales online or offline.
Engage builds repeat business, retention and advocacy over time.
Planning sets direction around these activities; RACE is not a promise that every individual follows a straight funnel.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: search visibility → product guide interaction → store purchase → helpful after-sale contact.
concepts.mistake: A newsletter signup is usually Act; it is not a sale just because analytics calls it a conversion event.
concepts.recall: In RACE, a prospect requests a product demonstration. Which stage is the closest fit?
answer: Name each RACE stage and purpose.
Distinguish lead interaction from sale.
Choose a stage-appropriate measure.

quiz.prompt: In RACE, a prospect requests a product demonstration. Which stage is the closest fit?
options: Engage, because every interaction is retention.
Act.
Convert, because every click is a sale.
explanations: Long-term retention differs from an initial prospect action.
A demo request is a meaningful interaction or lead.
RACE Convert refers to achieving sales.

concepts.definition: Sell, Speak, Serve, Save and Sizzle describe different benefits digital marketing can deliver.
points: Sell supports online and influenced offline sales.
Speak creates dialogue and customer understanding; Serve adds useful value.
Save reduces appropriate costs; Sizzle strengthens the brand experience.
Benefits can overlap; an objective needs a defined measure, baseline and timeframe.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: a self-service guide can Serve customers and Save support effort, but quality must be checked.
concepts.mistake: Reducing cost while making service unusable is not automatically a successful digital outcome.
concepts.recall: Which 5S best fits helping customers solve a product problem with a useful guide?
answer: Explain all five benefits.
Allow overlap where the mechanism supports it.
Give a measurable objective without inventing a business result.

quiz.prompt: Which 5S best fits helping customers solve a product problem with a useful guide?
options: Sell only.
Sizzle means counting every impression as profit.
Serve.
explanations: Support does not have to produce an immediate transaction.
Brand experience and profit are different outcomes.
The guide adds customer value; it may also save costs.

concepts.definition: An OVP explains the distinctive benefit of the online service in relation to the core offer, offline alternatives and competitors.
points: Segmentation, targeting and positioning still guide digital choices.
Useful content, convenience, interactivity and service can support differentiation.
The promise must be delivered by the experience and operations.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: reserve a stationery bundle online and collect it between classes, with confirmed stock.
concepts.mistake: “We are on the internet” does not explain a customer benefit or a competitive difference.
concepts.recall: Which is the strongest OVP for a campus retailer?
answer: Name the target need.
State a distinctive online benefit.
Explain how delivery supports the promise.

quiz.prompt: Which is the strongest OVP for a campus retailer?
options: Reserve confirmed stock online and collect in a chosen break.
We use the newest technology.
We have a website.
explanations: This states a relevant, deliverable customer benefit.
A technology label does not establish customer value.
Presence alone is not a value proposition.

concepts.definition: Assess the opportunity, choose a strategic approach, implement it, and use evidence to improve the plan.
points: Opportunity joins objectives, current performance and marketplace analysis.
Strategy selects target value and the communications mix.
Action delivers customer experience and integrated communications.
Profiling, measurement and improvement feed back into the earlier decisions.
Responsibilities, resources and clear objectives prevent disconnected experiments.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: investigate a weak checkout before increasing traffic; choose a relevant fix, test it and review results.
concepts.mistake: The textbook’s double-headed arrows mean this is not a one-pass checklist.
concepts.recall: Results contradict the campaign assumptions. What should the team do?
answer: Describe all three phases.
Include implementation and measurement.
Explain the feedback loop to objectives and strategy.

quiz.prompt: Results contradict the campaign assumptions. What should the team do?
options: Keep the plan unchanged until the year ends.
Use the evidence to revisit assumptions, objectives and execution.
Buy another platform without diagnosing the problem.
explanations: A rigid sequence ignores learning.
Measurement informs the next planning decisions.
New tools do not replace diagnosis.

concepts.definition: A digital presence can focus on transactions, relationship-building, brand-building, publishing/intermediation or community.
points: Transactional sites enable purchases and can also support offline sales.
Relationship-building sites generate leads and support complex purchases.
Brand sites develop an experience; publisher/intermediary sites organise content or comparisons.
Communities enable interactions among users.
Revenue may come from product sales, advertising, subscription or referral arrangements; functionality and revenue mechanism are different decisions.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: an equipment consultant uses a lead-generating site rather than forcing immediate checkout for a complex contract.
concepts.mistake: These are overlapping functions, not mutually exclusive company types.
concepts.recall: A complex B2B service website primarily generates qualified enquiries. Which function fits best?
answer: Explain the five functions.
Match functionality to buying needs.
Distinguish website purpose from revenue mechanism.

quiz.prompt: A complex B2B service website primarily generates qualified enquiries. Which function fits best?
options: Online checkout is always required.
A community must sell every post.
Services-oriented relationship-building.
explanations: Digital contribution can occur before an offline sale.
Community interaction has a different primary purpose.
Information and lead support suit a complex buying decision.

concepts.definition: Direct digital channels may grow demand through market expansion, brand switching or relationship deepening.
points: Market expansion brings in people who did not previously buy in the category.
Brand switching wins buyers from competitors.
Relationship deepening increases business with existing customers.
International reach still depends on local service, fulfilment and economics.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: an existing customer begins using a second relevant service after useful follow-up: relationship deepening.
concepts.mistake: A bigger audience is not evidence of profitable expansion, and every new-to-brand buyer is not new to the category.
concepts.recall: An existing customer purchases an additional relevant service. Which route fits?
answer: Distinguish category expansion, competitor switching and deeper relationships.
Identify what evidence would tell them apart.
Do not infer profitability from reach alone.

quiz.prompt: An existing customer purchases an additional relevant service. Which route fits?
options: Relationship deepening.
Market expansion in every case.
Brand switching in every case.
explanations: The relationship with an existing customer grows.
Market expansion concerns new category demand.
There is no evidence this transaction was won from a competitor.

concepts.definition: Digital opportunities require viable economics, relevant customer experience, clear ownership and operational capability.
points: Campaign complexity and platform changes need skills and maintenance.
Competition, acquisition costs and limited attention constrain results.
Poor objectives, fragmented budgets and missing measurement weaken strategy.
The Boo.com case links an ambitious experience and international rollout to technology, market and financial constraints.
concepts.example: Textbook historical case: Boo.com’s rich experience was difficult for many dial-up users; the chapter contrasts it with Boohoo’s later approach, while also discussing Boohoo’s 2020 supply-chain controversy.
concepts.mistake: Boohoo.com is not Boo.com renamed, and historical sales success does not establish ethical success.
concepts.recall: What is the strongest lesson from the chapter’s Boo.com case?
answer: Connect customer access, proposition, resources and economics.
Distinguish Boo.com from Boohoo.com.
Separate historical commercial evidence from ethical evaluation.

quiz.prompt: What is the strongest lesson from the chapter’s Boo.com case?
options: Good-looking technology alone ensures demand.
Validate customer experience and economics before scaling.
The two names describe the same company.
explanations: A compelling demonstration can still fail real users.
The case highlights multiple interdependent execution risks.
The source explicitly says the businesses are unrelated.

concepts.definition: B2B, B2C, C2C and C2B describe exchanges between businesses and consumers; public-service exchanges add government roles.
points: Identify both the supplier and the receiver of value.
Consumers may exchange information as well as money.
User-generated recommendations are important C2C interactions even on business-run platforms.
A business can serve several audience types; a demographic label does not establish a person’s needs.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: a student sells a used textbook to another student through a marketplace: C2C mediated by a business platform.
concepts.mistake: The platform owner’s identity does not automatically make every user-to-user exchange B2C.
concepts.recall: Two consumers exchange a used product on a business-run marketplace. What is the exchange?
answer: Identify the two transaction parties.
Explain the platform’s intermediary role.
Allow informational as well as financial exchanges.

quiz.prompt: Two consumers exchange a used product on a business-run marketplace. What is the exchange?
options: Always B2B.
Always government-to-consumer.
C2C.
explanations: The intermediary does not change the identities of the trading parties.
No government party is specified.
Both trading parties are consumers.

concepts.definition: Interactivity, intelligence, individualisation, integration, industry restructuring and independence of location describe opportunities of digital media.
points: Interactivity enables dialogue; intelligence uses interaction data for insight.
Individualisation tailors communication; integration connects channels.
Industry restructuring includes removal or creation of intermediaries.
Independence of location broadens reach but does not remove fulfilment or cultural constraints.
Testing, flexibility, accountability, targeting and cost control remain conditional capabilities.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: a firm combines web enquiries with phone support (integration), then personalises relevant follow-up (individualisation).
concepts.mistake: Digital media can push as well as pull; tracking does not automatically prove causation.
concepts.recall: A brand sells directly, bypassing a former distributor. Which change is this?
answer: Name the six opportunities.
Distinguish disintermediation from new intermediary creation.
State one practical limitation.

quiz.prompt: A brand sells directly, bypassing a former distributor. Which change is this?
options: Disintermediation within industry restructuring.
Individualisation only.
Proof that logistics no longer matters.
explanations: A former link between supplier and customer is removed.
Tailoring a message is a different mechanism.
Physical fulfilment can remain essential.

concepts.definition: Devices provide access; platforms mediate interactions. Selection depends on audience adoption, usage context and the task.
points: Assess device capability, timing, accessibility and connection conditions.
Device-specific targeting and dayparting adjust who is reached and when.
Sector-specific and regional platforms may matter more than a large global platform.
FAMGA is the textbook’s historical shorthand; it is not an up-to-date platform recommendation.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: test whether a target group can use an AR feature before choosing it for a campaign.
concepts.mistake: Growing up with digital media does not guarantee adoption of every new technology.
concepts.recall: Before an AR campaign, which evidence is most useful?
answer: Distinguish device and platform.
Assess capability and adoption in the target audience.
Connect context to the intended customer task.

quiz.prompt: Before an AR campaign, which evidence is most useful?
options: Only the creative team’s newest phone.
Target-audience access, supported devices and context of use.
A claim that all young people use the same platforms.
explanations: Internal equipment may not represent customers.
The intended audience must be able and willing to participate.
Age alone is an inadequate capability measure.

concepts.term: Media relationships and six channel families
concepts.definition: Paid, owned and earned describe media investment/control relationships; six channel families describe communication techniques.
points: Paid buys reach or response; owned is the brand’s managed presence; earned includes independent mentions and sharing.
The six families are search, social, digital/display advertising, digital PR, partnerships and messaging.
Search includes paid PPC and organic SEO; social includes paid and organic activity.
PR seeks and manages mentions; partnerships include affiliates or co-marketing; messaging includes email and push.
A relevant landing page continues the offer; organic activity still uses labour and production resources.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: a paid social ad promotes an owned guide that a customer independently shares; the three media types work together.
concepts.mistake: A paid influencer placement is not independent earned publicity just because an influencer published it.
concepts.recall: A brand pays a creator for a promotional placement. How should the placement be treated?
answer: Separate media relationship from channel family.
Identify payment and control.
Explain how one campaign can join paid, owned and earned.

quiz.prompt: A brand pays a creator for a promotional placement. How should the placement be treated?
options: Automatically earned because a third party posts it.
Owned media because payment gives complete control of the platform.
Paid media in the relevant channel.
explanations: Third-party publication alone does not make publicity earned.
Paying for placement does not mean owning the platform.
Payment makes it a bought placement.

concepts.definition: Attract people who actively seek relevant information through content, search and social interactions.
points: Visibility matters at the moment of need.
Organic options avoid a direct media fee but still require work.
Inbound may offer less control over audience timing and scale than a push campaign.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: a useful comparison guide answers a searcher’s question and leads them to a relevant service.
concepts.mistake: Inbound is not a synonym for every digital message or for marketing that costs nothing.
concepts.recall: Which activity most clearly follows an inbound approach?
answer: Explain proactive customer information seeking.
Name a relevant content/discovery mechanism.
State a control or cost limitation.

quiz.prompt: Which activity most clearly follows an inbound approach?
options: A searchable guide that answers a problem the audience is investigating.
An automatic guarantee of free customers.
An unsolicited interruption unrelated to the user’s task.
explanations: The user’s information need initiates the interaction.
Organic discovery is neither costless nor guaranteed.
This interrupts rather than responds to an expressed need.

concepts.definition: Seek agreement before developing a marketing relationship, usually by offering something useful in exchange.
points: Make the proposed communication and customer benefit understandable.
A subscription can be a lead, not a completed sale.
Respect communication preferences rather than assuming every interaction is permission.
This is the textbook’s marketing principle; current legal requirements need separate jurisdiction-specific verification.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: offer a study-planning guide and a clear optional newsletter subscription rather than hiding signup inside an unrelated action.
concepts.mistake: A public email address or a single visit is not the same as agreed marketing participation.
concepts.recall: Which action best reflects permission marketing?
answer: Explain the value exchange.
Make agreement and preferences explicit.
Distinguish permission from mere access to contact details.

quiz.prompt: Which action best reflects permission marketing?
options: Add every public address to the mailing list.
Explain the newsletter value and let the person choose to subscribe.
Treat viewing a product as consent to every message.
explanations: Availability of an address does not establish agreement.
This offers a clear voluntary exchange.
An interaction is not blanket permission.

concepts.definition: Plan, create, distribute and manage useful content to engage audiences and support business goals across relevant presences.
points: Choose content goals and formats for the customer’s lifecycle needs.
Plan distribution through search, social, partners and paid promotion.
Support interaction and moderate or respond to participation.
A branded hub makes relevant assets accessible.
People, processes, platforms and measurement sustain the content operation.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: a campus retailer organises buying guides in a resource hub, distributes selected answers through social posts, and uses questions to improve guides.
concepts.mistake: Publishing often is not a content strategy unless content, distribution and outcomes fit together.
concepts.recall: Which plan is closest to a complete content approach?
answer: Join audience need and business purpose.
Include format, distribution and participation.
Assign ownership and measures.

quiz.prompt: Which plan is closest to a complete content approach?
options: Count files in a folder as customer engagement.
Post every day without a purpose.
Create a useful guide, distribute it appropriately and measure relevant interactions.
explanations: Stored assets do not prove that an audience used them.
Frequency alone does not establish value.
Creation, distribution and review work together.

concepts.definition: Repeated interactions across the relationship can deepen customers’ involvement with a brand over time.
points: A click, comment or visit is a short-term interaction.
Sustained involvement, retention and advocacy require evidence across time.
An integrated lifecycle plan and coherent customer view help maintain relevant contact.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: a customer uses support, returns for a relevant purchase and independently recommends the brand over several months.
concepts.mistake: A high like count does not by itself demonstrate durable engagement or loyalty.
concepts.recall: Which is stronger evidence of long-term engagement?
answer: Distinguish an event from a relationship.
Look for repeated relevant interactions across time.
Avoid treating reactions as automatic loyalty or profit.

quiz.prompt: Which is stronger evidence of long-term engagement?
options: Relevant repeated interactions and retention over time.
The number of accounts the brand creates.
One popular post alone.
explanations: This fits the relationship perspective.
Brand activity is not the same as customer involvement.
One event cannot establish durability.

concepts.definition: Continuously plan and optimise useful acquisition and retention activities alongside time-limited campaigns.
points: Examples include useful search content, onboarding and service follow-up.
Triggers should fit customer behaviour, needs and preferences.
Retargeting revisits prior interactors; it is not proof of customer interest or permission for every use.
Continuous activity still requires monitoring, resources and a stop/review policy.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: a chosen welcome sequence helps subscribers use a service, while a separate launch campaign introduces a new feature.
concepts.mistake: Always-on does not mean message everyone constantly or automate without review.
concepts.recall: Which plan fits always-on lifecycle marketing?
answer: Contrast a continuous lifecycle activity with a campaign burst.
Tie a trigger to a relevant need.
Explain monitoring and preference safeguards.

quiz.prompt: Which plan fits always-on lifecycle marketing?
options: A single launch poster only.
A monitored onboarding sequence supporting new customers throughout the year.
Unlimited repeated messages regardless of response.
explanations: A burst can complement but does not constitute always-on activity.
This serves an ongoing lifecycle need.
Constant volume can damage relevance and the customer relationship.

concepts.definition: Profiles describe customer characteristics and preferences; behavioural data describes interactions. Inferred values are estimates rather than disclosed facts.
points: Disclosed details include contact information the person supplies.
Behavioural information may include pages viewed, visits and purchases.
Communication preferences describe desired contact.
Data lakes retain diverse raw data; warehouses hold structured data.
Check quality, purpose and appropriate access before using data.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: an email address is disclosed profile data, a guide view is behaviour, and predicted lifetime value is an inference.
concepts.mistake: A prediction about value or intent is not something the customer necessarily told the business.
concepts.recall: Which item is inferred rather than directly disclosed?
answer: Separate profile and behaviour.
Identify an inferred estimate.
Explain why data quality and customer preferences matter.

quiz.prompt: Which item is inferred rather than directly disclosed?

concepts.definition: Analyse digital interactions to assess and improve their contribution to business and customer goals.
points: Define a question and relevant metric before collecting everything.
Check tracking quality, device context and consistent denominators.
Use insights to choose an action and review its outcome.
The scope includes reach, referrals, behaviour, satisfaction, leads and sales, not only website traffic.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: investigate whether mobile enquiry completion differs from desktop, check measurement quality and test a relevant form improvement.
concepts.mistake: A dashboard full of numbers is not automatically actionable insight, and correlation does not establish cause.
concepts.recall: Which question best uses digital analytics?
answer: Start with a decision and objective.
Choose and validate relevant measures.
State how the result informs improvement.

quiz.prompt: Which question best uses digital analytics?
options: Where does the enquiry journey lose users, and what evidence supports a fix?
Can any traffic increase be declared profit?
How many numbers can we display?
explanations: The question connects measurement to a decision.
Traffic and profit are different measures.
Volume of metrics is not the objective.

concepts.definition: Assess how different media touchpoints contribute to conversions and value across a customer journey.
points: A purchase may follow several visits and channels.
Cross-device use and missing tracking can obscure the path.
A crediting rule is an analytical choice, not direct proof of causal impact.
Review channel interaction rather than assuming the final click did all the work.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: a person discovers a brand through social content, later searches, and finally responds to an email before buying.
concepts.mistake: Giving the final email all credit does not prove earlier interactions were irrelevant.
concepts.recall: A purchase follows social discovery, search and email. What is the careful conclusion?
answer: Describe the multi-touch journey.
Explain what attribution seeks to assess.
State tracking and causal limitations.

quiz.prompt: A purchase follows social discovery, search and email. What is the careful conclusion?
options: The last click proves all earlier channels had zero value.
Different touches may contribute; the crediting method and tracking limits matter.
All channels must receive identical credit in every business.
explanations: The final recorded event does not rule out earlier contribution.
This separates analytical credit from certainty about cause.
Equal weighting is a possible rule, not a universal truth.

concepts.definition: Software and services support marketing operations, customer experiences, communications and insight.
points: Operational tools deliver and manage activities.
Insight tools support analysis and reporting; many tools combine both.
SaaS provides software functionality through hosted services.
Tool selection follows goals, capabilities, integration needs and total cost.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: use a content system and a small analytics setup to answer a defined need before considering more specialised tools.
concepts.mistake: More tools or fashionable AI features do not by themselves establish return on investment.
concepts.recall: What should lead martech selection?
answer: Connect the tool to an objective.
Distinguish insight and operational roles.
Consider integration, people and cost.

quiz.prompt: What should lead martech selection?
options: The assumption that automation always raises profit.
The size of a vendor’s logo collection.
A clear need, expected contribution and implementation capability.
explanations: Automation needs relevant data, rules and ongoing review.
Popularity alone does not establish fit.
Technology should serve the plan and the organisation.

concepts.definition: The chapter’s Figure 1.13 groups technology into experiences, operations, middleware, backbone platforms, infrastructure and internet platforms.
points: Experiences include customer-facing content, service and testing.
Operations include analytics, attribution, dashboards and assets.
Middleware joins systems through APIs, tagging and identity/data handling.
Backbone platforms include CRM, content management, automation and e-commerce.
Infrastructure provides databases, cloud and development; internet platforms support interactions.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: a CRM backbone supplies a useful service context through middleware to a customer experience, while operations review performance.
concepts.mistake: This is a conceptual map from the source, not a current vendor ranking or a mandatory shopping list.
concepts.recall: Which layer primarily joins systems through APIs and data management?
answer: Identify all six groups.
Explain one relationship between them.
State why the diagram is not a product recommendation.

quiz.prompt: Which layer primarily joins systems through APIs and data management?
options: Marketing middleware.
Only the visible campaign artwork.
Only the internet audience.
explanations: The middleware layer connects services and information.
Artwork is not system integration.
An audience is not an integration layer.

concepts.definition: Realising technology value requires clear responsibilities, reliable data, connected processes and ongoing improvement.
points: APIs provide defined ways for systems to exchange information.
Assign responsibility for data quality, communications rules and performance.
Pilot a focused use case and evaluate the customer experience.
Consider operating effort and access controls as well as subscription cost.
concepts.example: Hypothetical: test one welcome flow using agreed preferences and consistent records before linking every system.
concepts.mistake: A successful data connection does not establish that every use of that data is appropriate or useful.
concepts.recall: What is the strongest implementation approach?
answer: Define the use case and owner.
Check data and process handoffs.
Pilot, evaluate and improve.

quiz.prompt: What is the strongest implementation approach?
options: Connect every system and decide the purpose later.
Pilot an owned use case with agreed data rules and outcome checks.
Treat a subscription receipt as proof of success.
explanations: Complexity without purpose can amplify errors.
This joins technology, process and customer value.
Spending measures cost, not the resulting benefit.

models.title: RACE: a lifecycle view
rows: Become aware and arrive at a relevant presence
Complete a sale online or offline
Continue a valuable relationship over time
Repeat sales, retention, advocacy and satisfaction
models.limit: A guide to planning and measurement, not a fixed path every person must follow. An analytics conversion event is not always a RACE sale.

models.title: 5Ss: a business-benefit view
rows: Grow relevant sales, including offline sales influenced online
An online enquiry leads to a useful store purchase
Create dialogue and learn about customers
Use volunteered questions to improve a service
A clear troubleshooting guide resolves a problem
Reduce suitable costs while maintaining value
A useful interactive experience expresses the brand promise
models.limit: The benefits overlap. Choose a baseline, a defined measure and a timeframe; these examples claim no achieved business result.

models.title: 6Is: communications opportunities
rows: Reliable collection and interpretation are necessary
Content can be tailored to needs or behaviour
Relevance depends on data and an appropriate use
Online and offline touchpoints can work together
Intermediaries may be removed or newly created
A new intermediary can become a new dependency
Communications can reach new geographical markets
Delivery, localisation and support still constrain the offer
models.limit: These are opportunities rather than automatic advantages or proof of effectiveness.

models.title: Six channel families × media relationships
rows: Creative hosted on the brand website

models.limit: Original teaching examples. Classify the actual arrangement by payment and control; a family does not belong exclusively to one media type. Organic work still has production and staff costs.

historical.title: Burger King: connect interaction to trial
historical.text: The chapter describes a Brazilian AR campaign that invited people to interact through the app and offered a product incentive. It is useful for connecting an Act-stage interaction to trial and ongoing app use.
historical.limit: Campaign aims are not independently verified achieved results. The example does not show that AR suits every audience.

historical.title: Zalando: growth needs more than visibility
historical.period: Historical textbook account using sources through 2020
historical.text: The chapter links expansion to localisation, customer experience, paid visibility and distribution capability. It also notes the investment required before break-even in core markets.
historical.limit: Historical scale figures are not current facts or a forecast for another retailer. Local operations and economics matter.

historical.title: Boo.com and Boohoo.com: compare assumptions
historical.period: Boo.com, 1998–2000; Boohoo comparison uses sources through 2020
historical.text: Boo.com aimed for a rich global shopping experience, but its technology, realistic user access, rollout costs and commercial assumptions presented serious constraints. The later Boohoo.com is a different business. Its historical growth discussion includes targeting, media, customer experience and data, followed by a discussion of supply-chain allegations in 2020.
historical.limit: This is a historical, multi-factor case rather than proof of one cause. Commercial growth does not settle ethical evaluation, and the textbook does not establish either business’s current position.

fieldwork.title: Map a real C2C interaction
fieldwork.task: Record an actual example you have observed. Identify who creates the information, who receives it and how it might help or harm a business. Separate your observation from an inferred outcome.

fieldwork.title: Trace a mixed-channel journey
fieldwork.task: Observe or interview someone about a real purchase journey. Map online and offline contacts, handoffs and support. Do not invent interview findings.

fieldwork.title: Check device and platform fit
fieldwork.task: For one target audience, list the device capabilities and platform-use questions you need to answer. Collect dated sources or observations rather than assuming adoption.

fieldwork.title: Audit a small martech use case
fieldwork.task: Choose one real marketing task. Record a vendor’s current stated function, the date and URL you checked, the required data and integration, and what remains unverified. This site supplies no current vendor ranking.
